Adam Smith’s “Optimistic Deism,” 
the Invisible Hand of Providence, 
and the Unhappiness of Nations
Terry Peach
The question of whether Adam Smith subscribed to some version of what 
I call “optimistic deism” (in short) is one to which there is no agreed 
answer. For some scholars, following the early lead of T. E. Cliffe Les-
lie, both The Theory of Moral Sentiments and The Wealth of Nations are 
informed by Smith’s “theological conception of ‘that great, benevolent, 
and all-wise being . . . who is determined to maintain . . . at all times the 
greatest possible quantity of happiness’” (Cliffe Leslie 1888, 26). 1 For 
others, the optimistic deism was either confined to The Theory of Moral 
Sentiments, thus raising the possibility of a fundamental inconsistency 
between Smith’s two major works (Viner 1928; Grampp 1948), or it was 
merely affected in the earlier work, possibly for rhetorical or prudential

objective of producing the greatest possible quantity of happiness, deliberately implanted the 
necessary sentiments and propensities in human nature at the time of the creation.”

2. “Smith’s invisible hand was the hand of a divine providence” (Fitzgibbons 1995, 89; cf. 
Hill 2001, 22; and Denis 2005, 2). Even commentators such as Peter Minowitz (1993, 114) 
and István Hont (2005, 91) who are skeptical of Smith’s optimistic deism have allowed that 
the “hand” was represented by him as the appendage of a deistic Providence or God.
3. Other possibilities that have been suggested are that Smith later changed his mind but 
failed to revise the text of The Theory of Moral Sentiments  (Fleischacker 2004, 104, 108) and 
that “happiness” should be redefined (in effect) as “less miserable” (Rasmussen 2006). On 
Rasmussen’s interpretation, see footnote 47.
considerations (Griswold 1999, 332–33, 324–29, 361; Lindgren 1973, 148; 
Minowitz 1993, 2004). Yet another view is of a severely conflicted Smith 
who simultaneously believed and disbelieved in optimistic deism, even in 
The Theory of Moral Sentiments (Alvey 2003, 263–64, 267, 289).
One alleged manifestation of Smith’s (disputed) belief is the famous 
“invisible hand/Providence” story in part 4, chapter 1, of The Theory 
of Moral Sentiments , which ends with Smith concluding that “in ease 
of body and peace of mind, all the different ranks of life are nearly upon 
a level, and the beggar, who suns himself by the side of the highway, 
possesses that security which kings are fighting for” (TMS IV.I.10, 185). 
For supporters of an optimistic-deism reading, the invisible hand was 
evidently a reference to the hand of a divine Providence,2 which ensures 
that “real happiness” (“ease of body and peace of mind”) is dispensed to 
all regardless of rank and material wealth, with the “beggar” invoked as a 
colorful representative of the poor and lowly (Denis 2005, 2).
As others have recognized, however, a major problem for an “opti -
mistic” interpretation is that Smith’s account of the effects of “bettering 
our condition” in The Theory of Moral Sentiments (and in The Wealth of 
Nations) tends to suggest that nearly “all the different ranks of life” are 
sacrificing their “real happiness,” which, if true, might suggest that Smith 
really was “conflicted” (Alvey 2003) or that the optimistic deism was 
merely a rhetorical gloss (Griswold 1999).3
I will argue in this essay that there is indeed a direct conflict between 
the optimistic reading of The Theory of Moral Sentiments, and the invisi-
ble hand/Providence story in particular, and Smith’s account of the conse-
quences of “bettering our condition” (and other aspects of life in “commer-
cial society”) in his two major works. I suggest, however, that the apparent 
optimism of Smith’s invisible hand tale was a carefully crafted illusion or 
deception on his part, obtained by accentuating one, relatively unimportant 
influence on “bettering our condition” (the fascination with well-crafted 
devices), by not actually specifying the level of happiness on which “all the 
different ranks of life are nearly upon,” and by disguising the identities of

the beggar and the king at the conclusion of the story. I will argue that if 
the beggar is identified as Diogenes the Cynic, then the concealed mes-
sage, that the sustained enjoyment of “real happiness” is restricted mainly 
to the “wise and virtuous,” was anything but optimistic. 
As to why Smith should have attempted to conceal his true position, 
I propose that he was feigning consistency with a “deistic” theme that 
surfaces at repeated intervals throughout The Theory of Moral Senti-
ments. However, if consistency could be purchased only by intentional 
deception or concealment on Smith’s part, then I suggest that the status 
of the whole deistic apparatus is called into question. Thus, while the 
interpretation offered here may go some way toward resolving alleged 
tensions or contradictions in Smith’s thought—by suggesting that Smith 
was consistently pessimistic about the prospects for “real happiness”—it 
does so by raising other conundrums, not least of which is the sincerity 
of Smith’s commitment to any sort of deism.
The article proceeds as follows. The first section gives a preliminary 
reading of the invisible hand/Providence story in The Theory of Moral 
Sentiments. I suggest that the argument is set up by Smith in such a way as 
to positively invite a deistic reading in which the invisible hand and Provi-
dence are synonymous allusions to the agency of a benevolent Deity, who 
has ordained both the propagation and happiness of the human species. To 
that extent, those who have interpreted the invisible hand/Providence 
argument as evidence of Smith’s optimistic deism could be said to have 
done so entirely in accordance with Smith’s own design.
I turn in the second section to the meaning of “real happiness” and doc-
ument the tension in The Theory of Moral Sentiments between the analysis 
of “bettering our condition” and the attainment of “real happiness” by 
nearly all in “the different ranks of life,” including the character of “pru-
dent man,” who is introduced by Smith in the sixth edition of the book.
In the third section I turn to Smith’s position on “happiness” in The 
Wealth of Nations. I suggest that the main difference with The Theory of 
Moral Sentiments is that the prospects for most people of gaining “real 
happiness” are presented as even more remote.
In the fourth section I return to the invisible hand/Providence story. By 
this stage an optimistic reading would raise acute problems of inconsis-
tency, both within The Theory of Moral Sentiments and with The Wealth 
of Nations. But, as I argue, the optimism may be attributed to well-crafted 
ambiguity and subterfuge, undertaken to encourage a deistic reading of 
the text that did not reflect Smith’s own convictions.

4. The “principle” of our attraction to “systems” or “machines” for their own intrinsic 
properties, rather than their “utility” qua “ends” they are designed to promote, was a favorite 
Smithian theme, dating back (in print) to his Essays on Philosophical Subjects (see Smith 
1980, 45–46, 66).
5. Ease of body and tranquillity (or peace) of mind correspond to Smith’s conception of 
“real happiness,” discussed further in the following section.
In the final section I summarize the main argument of the article and 
offer concluding observations. 
On Providence and the Invisible Hand  
in The Theory of Moral Sentiments:  
An “Optimistic” Reading
The references in The Theory of Moral Sentiments to Providence and 
the invisible hand are in chapter 1 of part 4, “Of the Effect of Utility 
upon the Sentiment of Approbation,” in which Smith proclaims his insight 
that the “happy contrivance of any production of art [is] often more val-
ued, than the very end for which it was intended” (TMS IV.I.3, 179). To 
take the example of watches, their sole end (“utility,” as Smith uses the 
term) is time-keeping, yet watches are said to be desired more for their 
“perfection” (aesthetic qualities) as a piece of machinery (or “system”). 
“Nor,” Smith pronounces, “is it only with regard to . . . frivolous objects 
that our conduct is influenced by this principle; it is often the secret motive 
of the most serious and important pursuits of both private and public life” 
(TMS I V.I.7, 181).4
As an example of a more “serious and important” influence, we are 
then introduced to a “poor man’s son” who, believing that riches will 
confer “happiness and tranquillity” (TMS IV.I.8, 181), sacrifices his own 
happiness and tranquillity in order to attain them, only to discover “in 
the last dregs of life” that “wealth and greatness are mere trinkets of frivo-
lous utility, no more adapted for procuring ease of body or tranquillity of 
mind5 than the tweezer-cases of the lover of toys” (181). Having realized 
that the trappings of wealth “can afford him no real satisfaction,” he at 
last sees power and riches for what they really are:
enormous and operose machines contrived to produce a few trifling con-
veniences to the body, consisting of springs the most nice and delicate, 
which must be kept in order with the most anxious attention. . . . They 
are immense fabrics, which it requires the labour of a life to raise, which 
threaten every moment to overwhelm the person that dwells in them. . . .

6. The philosophically informed spectator would not imagine “that they possess more 
means of happiness” in the sense of real happiness (see below). Smith corrects himself in the 
sentence immediately following: “And it is the ingenious and artful adjustment of those 
means to the end for which they [“the numberless artificial and elegant contrivances”] were 
intended, that is the principal source of his admiration.” The quality of being “admirable” to 
a detached spectator is not the same as being a source of “real happiness.”
They keep off the summer shower, not the winter storm, but leave him 
always as much, and sometimes more exposed than before, to anxiety, to 
fear, and to sorrow; to diseases, to danger, and to death. (182–83)
It would seem that the mistake had been to confound the “beauty” of the 
elements of wealth with the happiness that their possession would con -
fer. But that is not quite the whole explanation.
Having described the poor man’s son’s “ambition” in terms of the “prin-
ciple” of infatuation with “the exact adjustment of the means for attaining 
any conveniency or pleasure,” Smith introduces “vanity,” if only briefly, to 
explain why some “means” are preferred to others. On this account, “the 
palaces, the gardens, the equipage, the retinue of the great,” are more “rea-
sonable subjects of vanity” than “a tooth-pick [or] a machine for cutting 
the nails” because they “more effectually gratify that love of distinction so 
natural to man” (182). However, perhaps to dispel any suspicion that social 
distinction is itself the object of vanity and ambition, independently of the 
imagined happiness from the material “subjects of vanity,” a “spectator” 
fleetingly appears to assure us that the condition of the rich and great is 
admired “upon account . . . of the numberless artificial and elegant con-
trivances [they possess] for promoting . . . ease or pleasure.” This “specta-
tor” does not imagine that the rich and great “are really happier than other 
people”; rather, they only “possess more means of happiness” (182). 6 
Unfortunately, not least for the poor man’s son, the spectator’s “abstract 
and philosophical” view of wealth is rarely adopted (by nonphilosophers) 
except in “time of sickness or low spirits.” In “better health and in better 
humour,” we are duped by our admiration of “artificial and elegant con-
trivances” into thinking that the “pleasures of wealth and greatness [are] 
something grand and beautiful and noble, of which the attainment is well 
worth all the toil and anxiety which we are apt to bestow upon it” (TMS 
IV.I.9, 183). Smith continued:
And it is well that nature imposes on us in this manner. It is this 
deception which rouses and keeps in continual motion the industry of 
mankind. It is this which first prompted them to cultivate the ground,

to build houses, to found cities and commonwealths, and to invent and 
improve all the sciences and arts, which ennoble and embellish human 
life; which have entirely changed the whole face of the globe, have 
turned the rude forests of nature into agreeable and fertile plains. . . . 
The earth by these labours of mankind has been obliged to redouble her 
natural fertility, and to maintain a greater multitude of inhabitants. 
(TMS I V.I.10, 183 – 84)
So, “nature” has purposefully implanted the “deception” that “wealth and 
greatness” bring happiness in order to stimulate industry and provide for 
an expanding population; and the mechanism by which the trick is worked 
involves a conflation of the happiness from wealth and greatness with the 
aesthetic appeal of the “system” or manner of living (material possessions, 
domestic arrangements, and so forth) of the rich and great.
Having dispatched the poor man’s son to his twilight years of misery 
and remorse, Smith introduces a new character, “the proud and unfeeling 
landlord” (184). “It is to no purpose,” Smith declares, that this (as described) 
loathsome individual “views his extensive fields, and without a thought for 
the wants of his brethren, in imagination consumes himself the whole har-
vest that grows upon them”:
The capacity of his stomach bears no proportion to the immensity of his 
desires, and will receive no more than that of the meanest peasant. The 
rest he is obliged to distribute among those, who prepare, in the nicest 
manner, that little which he himself makes use of, among those who fit 
up the palace in which this little is to be consumed, among those who 
provide and keep in order all the different baubles and trinkets, which 
are employed in the oeconomy of greatness; all of whom thus derive 
from his luxury and caprice, that share of the necessaries of life, which 
they would in vain have expected from his humanity or his justice. (184)
It is unclear if the landlord is motivated by the same deception that beguiled 
the poor man’s son, although consistency within the chapter would seem to 
require that he is. We are told merely that he, and his class, exhibit “selfish-
ness and rapacity,” they “mean only their own conveniency,” and “the sole 
end which they propose [is] the gratification of their own vain and insatia-
ble desires” (184). It is not so much the motive as the consequence of their 
behavior that Smith stresses:
The rich . . . divide with the poor the produce of all their improvements. 
They are led by an invisible hand to make nearly the same distribution

been divided into equal portions among all its inhabitants, and thus 
without intending it, without knowing it, advance the interest of the 
society, and afford means to the multiplication of the species. (184–85)7
The landlords’ wealth derives from the produce of their land. They make 
“improvements” not with a nonsensical desire to consume more of the 
increased produce of their land themselves,8 nor with a philanthropic urge 
to feed the poor and “afford means to the multiplication of the species,” 
but to indulge their “vain and insatiable desires” for “artificial and elegant 
contrivances.” The only way they can satisfy their desires is by distribut-
ing “the necessaries of life” to the poor who maintain and supply the 
“contrivances.”
Had Smith concluded on the point about the provision of necessaries 
he would have produced an argument that anticipated the one he developed 
in The Wealth of Nations (cf. Winch 1978, 92), the principal difference 
being that the earlier version in The Theory of Moral Sentiments linked the 
benefits to the poor with the luxury consumption of the rich, whereas The 
Wealth of Nations version linked them with the investment decisions of 
rich merchants.9 But Smith did not conclude at this point.10 He continued:

When Providence divided the earth among a few lordly masters, it nei-
ther forgot nor abandoned those who seemed to have been left out in the 
partition. These last too enjoy their share of all that it produces. In what 
constitutes the real happiness of human life, they are in no respect infe-
rior to those who would seem so much above them. In ease of body and 
peace of mind, all the different ranks of life are nearly upon a level, and 
the beggar, who suns himself by the side of the highway, possesses that 
security which kings are fighting for. (TMS IV.I.10, 185)
Here the argument shifts from the distribution of “necessaries” to the 
providential dispensation of “the real happiness of human life,” as asso-
ciated (in the sentence immediately following) with “ease of body and 
peace of mind.” But what level of “real happiness” are all the “differ -
ent ranks . . . nearly upon”? And why, suddenly, are we invited to pon -
der a comparison between a seemingly contented beggar and insecure 
monarchs?
Smith does not answer those questions explicitly. It is as if readers are 
invited to place their own construction on his pronouncement: they can 
put the “level” almost anywhere they wish. Admittedly, some candidates 
for “real happiness” have been ruled out, among them the poor man’s son 
and insecure kings, but the possibility appears to have been left open that 
many others, including the poor who supply and maintain “contrivances,” 
may enjoy the “real happiness” of the carefree beggar.
“And it is well,” one might say, that Smith “imposes on us in this man-
ner,” because he can thereby intimate a connection with a theme that runs 
throughout The Theory of Moral Sentiments : the consistency of human 
behavior with the plan, or “system,” of a benevolent Deity.11
The references to the invisible hand and Providence are in consecutive 
sentences, suggesting that they were intended to be read (and certainly 
have been read)12 as synonymous allusions to the same entity, one that has 
as its objective “the multiplication of the species” and “the real happiness 
of human life.” It requires no forensic skill to uncover the identity of such 
an entity in The Theory of Moral Sentiments: it is “the Deity,” the “Author” 
and “great Director of the universe,” the “Great Judge of Hearts” and “all-
seeing Judge of the world,” “God,” who has ordained both the “great ends” 
(including “self-preservation,” “the propagation of the species,” and, most

Smith had crafted a seductive (if not entirely original) 15 story which

gar. In the following section I consider more closely Smith’s conception of 
“real happiness” and assess the extent to which the optimistic reading of 
the invisible hand/Providence story is borne out elsewhere in The Theory 
of Moral Sentiments. 
Real Happiness and “Bettering Our Condition”
The identification of “real happiness” with “ease of body and peace of 
mind” (or “tranquillity of mind”) had an Epicurean ring to it, unsurpris-

tion of The Theory of Moral Sentiments, “Of Systems of Moral Philoso-
phy” (TMS VII.ii.2.7). In opposition to Epicurus, however, Smith followed 
Francis Hutcheson (1755, 1:23–24, 148) in maintaining that “real happi-
ness” cannot be reduced to a metric of (bodily) pleasure and pain (TMS 
VII.ii.2.13–17). Rather, as many commentators have recognized,16 it is on

The inclusion of “ease of body” marked a departure from received Stoic 
teaching, perhaps suggested to Smith from his reading of Cicero.19 Never-
theless, having allowed that food, clothing, and shelter are required for 
“real happiness” (they are the material conditions for “ease of body”), 
Smith takes the Stoic line20 that these “necessities of nature” can be sup-

I.iii.2.1, 50).21 “Real happiness” does not increase with material consump-

We are left with the second and, on Smith’s (and the Stoics’) account, by 
far the more important component of “real happiness”: peace and tranquil-

tranquillity required for “real happiness”23—it must be associated with vir-

Smith had a dilemma. Having embraced a basically Stoic conception of 
happiness that placed the emphasis on tranquillity of mind, and having 
concluded that such tranquillity was not generally experienced by all the 
“different ranks,” he could either make his view clear, thereby casting 
doubt on the “infinite perfections” and very existence of a benevolent 
Deity, or he could obscure his position. He chose the latter, artfully con-
cocting a form of words that could, and would, be read as suggesting a 
view he could not personally endorse, leaving his reservations encoded in 
a recondite classical allusion.
Conclusion
On the interpretation offered here, the “complacent ‘providentialism’” 
(Winch 1978, 92) of the invisible hand/Providence story was in large part 
an illusion (save for the claim about “ease of body”): an illusion created 
by emphasizing the deceptive “love of system” (the fascination with well-
crafted contrivances) as the main spur to material acquisitiveness; by 
using the empty formulation that “all the different ranks of life are nearly 
upon a level” without specifying which level they are “nearly upon”; and 
by introducing a contented beggar who, with his identity as Diogenes the 
Cynic cloaked in anonymity, could be tendentiously misconstrued as a 
representative of the poor and lowly. 
Taking The Theory of Moral Sentiments as a whole, “love of system” 
pales into insignificance compared with vanity, emulation, and the desire 
for social status, which stand out as the main inducements for “bettering our
